summary: Describes the architecture of Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS). It extends label switching beyond packet routers to optical and transmission equipment such as DWDM systems and cross-connects, so the network can set up paths dynamically and recover from failures.

plainLanguage.summary: Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) extends MPLS control methods to networks that switch more than packets. It describes how routing, signaling and link management can establish paths through equipment that switches time slots, wavelengths or physical ports.

questions: what is lmp link management protocol
subtitle: The GMPLS control plane extends label switching to time slots, wavelengths and physical links.

tldr.problem: Traditional MPLS assumes that forwarding equipment can read packet or cell headers. Optical and transmission equipment can instead switch time slots, wavelengths or physical ports, and networks may have many parallel links between nodes.
tldr.mechanism: GMPLS extends MPLS signaling and routing, defines generalized labels and label requests, and adds unnumbered links, link bundling, forwarding adjacencies and the Link Management Protocol for control and scaling needs.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a control-plane architecture for packet, layer-2, time-division, wavelength and fiber switching. The unit metadata lists RFC 6002 as an update.

facts.label: Generic bandwidth encoding
facts.value: 32-bit IEEE floating point, bytes per second

today: RFC 3945 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists RFC 6002 as an update and lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Five Kinds of Switching Interface
sections.content:
Traditional MPLS assumes a device can recognize packet or cell boundaries and forward data based on a header. GMPLS also covers interfaces that switch on a repeating time slot, a wavelength or a physical port or fiber.

The RFC names five interface classes: Packet Switch Capable (PSC), Layer-2 Switch Capable (L2SC), Time-Division Multiplex Capable (TDM), Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) and Fiber-Switch Capable (FSC). A circuit through GMPLS is called a Label Switched Path (LSP), whatever name its technology uses for that circuit.

LSPs can be nested. The hierarchy runs from packet switching through layer 2 and TDM to wavelength and fiber switching, so a packet LSP can be carried inside paths at other layers.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS covers five switching interface types, from packet forwarding to switching whole fibers. A path at one type can be carried inside a path at a higher layer.

sections.title: The GMPLS Control Plane
sections.content:
The architecture separates a network's control plane from its forwarding plane. The control plane has a routing part and a signaling part. GMPLS generalizes MPLS and MPLS traffic engineering to support the five interface classes.

GMPLS extends RSVP-TE and CR-LDP for signaling, and OSPF-TE and IS-IS-TE for routing. It does not require one of the two signaling protocols over the other. The Link Management Protocol (LMP) is the specialized protocol introduced for managing links.

Labels can represent time slots, wavelengths or spatial positions, not only packet labels. GMPLS also supports bidirectional LSPs, label suggestions and restrictions, and rapid failure notification with RSVP-TE.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS keeps routing and signaling separate from data forwarding. It extends established routing and signaling protocols so they can request and manage paths in several kinds of networks.

sections.title: Routing, Unnumbered Links and Bundles
sections.content:
GMPLS reuses IP addressing and link-state routing to discover network topology and link resources. Traffic-engineering algorithms can use this information to find paths for circuits as well as IP data.

An unnumbered link has no IP address. Each endpoint assigns a local identifier, and the two endpoints exchange their identifiers. Link bundling lets several component links between the same pair of nodes be advertised as one logical traffic-engineering link, reducing routing information.

Components in a bundle must share their link type, traffic-engineering metric and resource classes at each end. The bundle is considered live while at least one component link is live. The upstream node chooses a component link and indicates that choice through a dedicated signaling channel, a numbered interface ID or an unnumbered interface ID.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS can identify a link with a local number instead of an IP address. It can also advertise similar parallel links together, then identify the particular component link when setting up a path.

sections.title: Managing Links with LMP
sections.content:
The control channel between two nodes does not have to use the same physical medium as their data links. Therefore, a working control channel does not prove that the data links are working. LMP manages links between data-plane neighbors independently of the links' transmission technology.

LMP's required procedures manage control channels and correlate link properties. Optional procedures verify data-link connectivity and manage faults. Control-channel management establishes and maintains channels; link-property correlation exchanges information used to form bundles and update traffic-engineering parameters.

Connectivity verification sends Test messages over data links. Fault management lets a downstream node report a data-link failure to an upstream node, which can localize it and start protection or restoration. The RFC also describes LMP-WDM exchanges between optical cross-connects and optical line systems.
sections.plainLanguage: LMP checks the control connection separately from the data links. It can also compare link details, test physical connectivity and report a failure to a neighboring node.

sections.title: Requesting a Generalized Path
sections.content:
To request an LSP, an ingress node sends a Path or Label Request downstream. A Generalized Label Request identifies the LSP encoding type, the switching type required on a link and the payload type. Technology-specific parameters can carry further details such as a signal type or bandwidth.

The downstream node replies with a Generalized Label. Depending on the layer, that label can identify a time slot, a wavelength, a fiber or another switching resource. Generic bandwidth uses a 32-bit IEEE floating-point value measured in bytes per second when technology-specific parameters are not used.

A bidirectional LSP is established with one set of signaling messages and an Upstream Label. GMPLS includes label suggestions to reduce setup delay and label sets to restrict choices, for example when wavelength conversion is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The request names the type of path and payload it needs. Each downstream node returns a label that identifies the resource it has selected, such as a time slot or wavelength.

sections.title: Forwarding Adjacencies and Recovery
sections.content:
A forwarding adjacency advertises an established LSP as a traffic-engineering link in OSPF or IS-IS. Other routers can use it for path computation and place their own LSPs inside it. This can reduce the forwarding state and signaling that intermediate routers need to maintain.

GMPLS distinguishes protection from restoration. Protection resources are established before a failure, and endpoints switch to them after a failure. Restoration uses signaling after the failure to find or activate a recovery path. The choices trade recovery speed, robustness and resource sharing.

Recovery includes fault detection, localization, notification, switching or restoration, and possibly returning traffic to a working path. The RFC cites a 50-millisecond SONET/SDH protection-switching objective, not including failure-detection time.
sections.plainLanguage: An established path can be advertised as a link for other paths to use. If a path fails, prearranged protection can switch traffic, while restoration finds or activates another route after the failure.

sections.title: Security for the Control Plane
sections.content:
GMPLS paths can carry large amounts of data and reserve significant network resources. The control plane therefore needs measures that reduce the risk of attackers injecting or observing control messages.

Risk depends on trust between nodes and on how the control channel is implemented. The RFC notes that an in-band channel in SONET/SDH overhead is generally considered less vulnerable than a control channel over an out-of-band IP network.

Component-protocol authentication or IPsec can provide authentication, and IPsec can also provide confidentiality. After verifying a requester's identity, control elements should check the request against local authorization policy. The RFC says GMPLS itself adds no security considerations beyond those of MPLS-TE signaling, routing protocols and SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized nodes should be able to request network resources. Control messages can be authenticated, and local policy can decide whether an authenticated requester may use the requested resources.
